examples.problem:
Negate the following statement: 

$\qquad$ Some quadrilaterals are squares.
examples.worked_solution:
Let $Q$ be the set of all quadrilaterals and $S$ the set of all squares. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\qquad$ There exists $q \in Q$ such that $q \in S$

Introducing the existential quantifier, we get the following:

$\qquad$ $\exists q \in Q, \, q \in S.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∃q\in Q,\,q\in S) & ≡∀q\in Q,\,¬(q\in S) \\  & ≡∀q\in Q,\,q\notin S\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\qquad$ For all $q \in Q,$ $q \not\in S.$

or simply

$\qquad$ All quadrilaterals are not squares.

feedback.problem:
Negate the following statement:

$\,$ Every sequence is arithmetic.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be the set of all sequences. The given statement can be re-phrased as follows:

$\,$ For all $s\in S,$ $s$ is arithmetic.

Introducing the universal quantifier, we get the following:

$\,$ $∀s\in S,\,s\text{ is arithmetic}.$

Negating this, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(∀s\in S,\,s\text{ is arithmetic}) & ≡∃s\in S,\,¬(s\text{ is arithmetic}) \\  & ≡∃s\in S,\,s\text{ is not arithmetic}\end{aligned}
$$

which reads 

$\,$ There exists $s\in S$ such that $s$ is not arithmetic.

or simply

$\,$ Some sequences are not arithmetic.
